danish.title: Ottende bog (1811–12) — Kapitel 8
paragraphs: Den aften tog Rostoverne i operaen, hvortil Marja Dmitrijevna havde skaffet en loge.

Natasja ville ikke af sted, men kunne ikke afslå Marja Dmitrijevnas venlige tilbud, der var tiltænkt netop hende. Da hun kom klædt på ind i salen for at vente på sin far og i det store spejl så, at hun var smuk, meget smuk, følte hun sig endnu mere trist, men det var en sød, øm tristhed.

»Åh Gud, hvis bare han var her nu, ville jeg ikke opføre mig som dengang, men anderledes. Jeg ville ikke være dum og bange, men simpelthen omfavne ham, klynge mig til ham og få ham til at se på mig med de søgende, spørgende øjne, han så tit har set på mig med, og så ville jeg få ham til at le, som han plejede at le. Og hans øjne — hvor jeg ser de øjne for mig!« tænkte Natasja. »Og hvad rager hans far og søster mig? Jeg elsker ham alene, ham, ham, med det ansigt og de øjne, med hans smil, mandigt og dog barnligt... Nej, jeg gør bedst i ikke at tænke på ham; ikke tænke på ham men glemme ham, helt glemme ham for nu. Jeg holder det ikke ud at vente, og straks bryder jeg ud i gråd!« og hun vendte sig bort fra spejlet og gjorde sig umage for ikke at græde. »Og hvordan kan Sonja elske Nikolaj så roligt og stille og vente så længe og så tålmodigt?« tænkte hun, idet hun kiggede på Sonja, der også kom ind helt klar, med en vifte i hånden. »Nej, hun er helt anderledes. Det kan jeg ikke!«

Natasja følte sig i det øjeblik så blødgjort og øm, at det ikke var nok for hende at elske og vide, at hun var elsket; hun ville nu, i dette øjeblik, omfavne den mand, hun elskede, tale og høre kærlighedsord fra ham, ord der fyldte hendes hjerte. Mens hun sad i vognen ved siden af sin far og eftertænksomt betragtede gadelygternes flammer flakke bag de frosne ruder, følte hun sig endnu tristere og mere forelsket og glemte, hvor hun var på vej hen, og med hvem. Da de var faldet ind i kareternes række, kørte Rostovernes vogn op til teatret, med hjulene knasende over sneen. Natasja og Sonja, der holdt deres kjoler op, sprang hurtigt ud. Greven steg ud med hjælp fra tjenerne, og idet de passerede mænd og kvinder, der gik ind, og programsælgerne, gik alle tre ned ad korridoren til den første række af loger. Gennem de lukkede døre var musikken allerede hørbar.
»Natasja, dit hår!...« hviskede Sonja.

En betjent gled ærbødigt og hurtigt foran damerne og åbnede døren til deres loge. Musikken lød højere, og gennem døren glitrede rækker af stærkt oplyste loger, hvori damer sad med bare arme og skuldre, og støjende parterre strålende af uniformer for deres øjne. En dame, der gik ind i nabologet, sendte et blik af kvindelig misundelse mod Natasja. Tæppet var endnu ikke gået op, og ouverturen spillede. Natasja glattede sin kjole, gik ind med Sonja og satte sig, mens hun lod blikket glide over de strålende logerækker overfor. En fornemmelse, hun ikke havde oplevet i lang tid — den af hundreder af øjne, der betragtede hendes bare arme og hals — påvirkede hende på én gang behageligt og ubehageligt og kaldte en hel skare af minder, ønsker og følelser forbundet med den fornemmelse frem.

De to bemærkelsesværdigt smukke piger, Natasja og Sonja, med grev Rostov, der ikke var blevet set i Moskva i lang tid, tiltrak sig alles opmærksomhed. Desuden vidste alle vagt besked om Natasjas forlovelse med fyrst Andrej og vidste, at Rostoverne havde boet på landet lige siden, og alle betragtede med nysgerrighed en brud, der var ved at gøre et af Ruslands bedste partier.

Natasjas udseende, som alle sagde, var blevet bedre på landet, og den aften var hun, takket være sin ophidselse, særlig smuk. Hun slog dem, der så hende, med sin livfuldhed og skønhed, kombineret med sin ligegyldighed over for alt omkring hende. Hendes sorte øjne betragtede mængden uden at søge nogen, og hendes sarte arm, bar til over albuen, hvilede på logens fløjlskant, mens hun, tydeligvis ubevidst, åbnede og lukkede sin hånd i takt med musikken og krøllede sit program. »Se, der er Alenina,« sagde Sonja, »med sin mor, ikke?«
»Herreje, Mikhail Kirillovitj er blevet endnu tykkere!« bemærkede greven.
»Se vores Anna Mikhajlovna — sikken en hovedpynt hun har på!«
»Karaginerne, Julie — og Boris med dem. Man kan straks se, at de er forlovede...«
»Drubetskoj har friet?«
»Åh ja, det hørte jeg i dag,« sagde Sjinsjin, der kom ind i Rostovernes loge.

Natasja kiggede i den retning, hendes fars øjne var vendt, og så Julie sidde ved siden af sin mor med et lykkeligt udtryk og en perlekæde om sin tykke, røde hals — som Natasja vidste var dækket af pudder. Bag dem, med et smil og bøjet over med øret mod Julies mund, sad Boris' smukke, glatkæmmede hoved. Han kiggede på Rostoverne under brynene og sagde noget med et smil til sin forlovede.
»De taler om os, om mig og ham!« tænkte Natasja. »Og han berolige sikkert hendes jalousi over mig. De behøver ikke bekymre sig! Hvis de bare vidste, hvor lidt jeg bryder mig om nogen af dem.«

Bag dem sad Anna Mikhajlovna med en grøn hovedpynt og et lykkeligt udtryk af hengivenhed til Guds vilje i ansigtet. Deres loge var gennemsyret af den atmosfære af et forlovet par, som Natasja kendte så godt og holdt så meget af. Hun vendte sig bort og huskede pludselig alt det, der havde været så ydmygende ved hendes morgenbesøg.

»Hvad ret har han til ikke at ville modtage mig i sin familie? Åh, lad mig hellere lade være med at tænke på det — ikke før han kommer!« sagde hun til sig selv og begyndte at kigge på ansigterne, nogle fremmede, nogle velkendte, i parterret. Forrest, midt for, med ryggen lænet mod orkesterrækværket, stod Dolokhov i persisk klædedragt med sit krøllede hår børstet op i en vældig tot. Han stod i fuld offentlighed, vel vidende at han tiltrak sig alles opmærksomhed, og dog lige så afslappet, som om han var i sit eget værelse. Omkring ham stimlede Moskvas mest strålende unge mænd, som han åbenbart dominerede.
Greven pegede leende den rødmende Sonja på hendes tidligere tilbeder.
»Genkender du ham?« sagde han. »Og hvor dukker han op fra?« spurgte han og vendte sig mod Sjinsjin. »Var han ikke forsvundet et sted?«

»Jo,« svarede Sjinsjin. »Han var i Kaukasus og flygtede derfra. De siger, han har fungeret som minister for en eller anden herskende fyrste i Persien, hvor han dræbte sjahen bror. Nu er alle Moskvas damer vanvittige med ham! Det er 'Dolokhov Perseren', der gør det! Vi hører ikke et ord, uden at Dolokhov nævnes. De sværger ved ham, de tilbyder ham som en lækker ret sterlet. Dolokhov og Anatol Kuragin har fuldstændig forvirret vore damer.«

En høj, smuk kvinde med en masse flettet hår og svulmende, hvide skuldre og hals, hvorom hun bar en dobbelt række store perler, trådte ind i nabologen med raslen af sin tunge silkekjole og brugte lang tid på at sætte sig til rette.

Natasja stirrede uvilkårligt på den hals, de skuldre, de perler og den frisure og beundrede skuldrenes og perlernes skønhed. Mens Natasja for anden gang fæstnede sit blik på hende, kiggede damen sig om, og idet hun mødte grevens øjne, nikkede hun til ham og smilede. Det var grevinde Bezukhova (Hélène), Pierres hustru, og greven, der kendte alle i selskabet, bøjede sig over og talte til hende.

»Har De været her længe, grevinde?« spurgte han. »Jeg kommer forbi, jeg kommer forbi for at kysse Deres hånd. Jeg er her i forretninger og har mine piger med. De siger, Semjonova spiller vidunderligt. Grev Pierre glemte os aldrig. Er han her?«
»Jo, han havde tænkt sig at kigge forbi,« svarede Hélène og kiggede opmærksomt på Natasja.
Grev Rostov satte sig igen.
»Smuk, ikke?« hviskede han til Natasja.
»Vidunderlig!« svarede Natasja. »Hun er en kvinde, man let kunne forelske sig i.«
Netop da hørtes ouverturens sidste akkorder, og dirigenten bankede med sin taktstok. Nogle sene gæster tog plads i parterret, og tæppet gik op.

Så snart det gik op, forstummede alle i logerne og parterret, og alle mændene, unge og gamle, i uniform og selskabstøj, og alle kvinderne med ædelstene på den bare hud rettede hele deres opmærksomhed med ivrig nysgerrighed mod scenen. Natasja begyndte også at kigge.

english.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: That evening the Rostovs went to the opera, for which Marya Dmitrievna had taken a box.

Natasha didn't want to go, but couldn't refuse Marya Dmitrievna's kind offer, which was intended specially for her. When she came out dressed and ready into the ballroom to wait for her father, and saw in the large mirror that she was pretty — very pretty — she felt even sadder, but it was a sweet, tender sadness.

"O God, if he were here now I wouldn't behave as I did then, but differently. I wouldn't be silly and afraid of things. I would simply embrace him, hold on to him, and make him look at me with those searching, inquiring eyes he so often turned on me, and then I would make him laugh as he used to laugh. And his eyes — how I see those eyes!" thought Natasha. "And what do his father and sister matter to me? I love him alone, him, him, with that face and those eyes, with his smile, manly and yet childlike... No, I'd better not think of him; not think of him but forget him, just forget him for now. I can't bear this waiting and I'll cry any minute!" and she turned away from the mirror, making an effort not to cry. "And how can Sonya love Nicholas so calmly and quietly and wait so long and so patiently?" she thought, looking at Sonya, who also came in all ready, with a fan in her hand. "No, she's completely different. I can't!"

Natasha at that moment felt so softened and tender that it wasn't enough for her to love and know she was loved — she wanted now, at once, to embrace the man she loved, to speak and hear from him words of love such as filled her heart. While she sat in the carriage beside her father, pensively watching the streetlamp lights flickering on the frozen window, she felt still sadder and more in love, and forgot where she was going and with whom. Having fallen into the line of carriages, the Rostovs' carriage drove up to the theater, its wheels squeaking over the snow. Natasha and Sonya, holding up their dresses, jumped out quickly. The count got out with the help of the footmen, and all three of them walked along the corridor to the first row of boxes.
"Natasha, your hair!..." whispered Sonya.

An attendant respectfully and quickly slipped ahead of the ladies and opened the door of their box. The music grew louder, and through the door rows of brightly lit boxes where ladies sat with bare arms and shoulders, and noisy stalls brilliant with uniforms, glittered before their eyes. A lady entering the next box shot a glance of feminine envy at Natasha. The curtain had not yet risen and the overture was being played. Natasha, smoothing her gown, went in with Sonya and sat down, scanning the brilliant tiers of boxes opposite. A sensation she hadn't experienced for a long time — that of hundreds of eyes looking at her bare arms and neck — suddenly affected her both pleasantly and unpleasantly and called up a whole crowd of memories, desires, and emotions connected with that feeling.

The two remarkably pretty girls, Natasha and Sonya, with Count Rostov, who had not been seen in Moscow for a long time, attracted general attention. Moreover, everybody knew vaguely of Natasha's engagement to Prince Andrew, and knew that the Rostovs had been living in the country ever since, and all looked with curiosity at a fiancee who was making one of the best matches in Russia.

Natasha's looks, as everyone told her, had improved in the country, and that evening, thanks to her excitement, she was especially pretty. She struck those who saw her by her fullness of life and beauty, combined with her indifference to everything around her. Her dark eyes looked at the crowd without seeking anyone, and her slender arm, bare above the elbow, lay on the velvet edge of the box, while she unconsciously opened and closed her hand in time to the music, crumpling her program. "Look, there's Alenina," said Sonya, "with her mother, isn't it?"
"My goodness, Michael Kirilovich has gotten even stouter!" remarked the count.
"Look at our Anna Mikhaylovna — what a headdress she has on!"
"The Kargins, Julie — and Boris with them. You can tell at once that they're engaged..."
"Drubetskoy has proposed?"
"Oh yes, I heard it today," said Shinshin, coming into the Rostovs' box.

Natasha looked in the direction her father's eyes were turned and saw Julie sitting beside her mother with a happy look on her face and a string of pearls around her thick red neck — which Natasha knew was covered with powder. Behind them, wearing a smile and leaning over with an ear to Julie's mouth, was Boris's handsome, neatly groomed head. He looked at the Rostovs from under his brows and said something, smiling, to his fiancee.
"They are talking about us, about me and him!" thought Natasha. "And he's probably calming her jealousy of me. They needn't worry! If only they knew how little I care about any of them."

Behind them sat Anna Mikhaylovna wearing a green headdress and with a happy look of resignation to God's will on her face. Their box was filled with that atmosphere of an engaged couple that Natasha knew so well and liked so much. She turned away and suddenly remembered everything that had been so humiliating about her morning visit.

"What right has he not to receive me into his family? Oh, better not think of it — not till he comes back!" she told herself, and began looking at the faces, some familiar and some strange, in the stalls. In the front, in the very center, leaning back against the orchestra rail, stood Dolokhov in a Persian outfit, his curly hair brushed up into a huge shock. He stood in full view of the audience, well aware that he was attracting everyone's attention, yet as relaxed as if he were in his own room. Around him crowded Moscow's most brilliant young men, whom he clearly dominated.
The count, laughing, nudged the blushing Sonya and pointed to her former admirer.
"Do you recognize him?" said he. "And where has he come from?" he asked, turning to Shinshin. "Didn't he disappear somewhere?"

"He did," replied Shinshin. "He was in the Caucasus and ran away from there. They say he's been acting as minister to some ruling prince in Persia, where he killed the Shah's brother. Now all the Moscow ladies are crazy about him! It's 'Dolokhov the Persian' that does it! You can't hear a word without Dolokhov being mentioned. They swear by him, they offer him to you like a dish of choice sturgeon. Dolokhov and Anatole Kuragin have turned all our ladies' heads."

A tall, beautiful woman with a mass of plaited hair and much exposed plump white shoulders and neck, around which she wore a double string of large pearls, entered the adjoining box, rustling her heavy silk dress, and took a long time settling into her seat.

Natasha involuntarily gazed at that neck, those shoulders, and pearls, and admired the beauty of the shoulders and the pearls. While Natasha was looking at her for the second time, the lady looked around and, meeting the count's eyes, nodded to him and smiled. She was Countess Bezukhova, Pierre's wife, and the count, who knew everyone in society, leaned over and spoke to her.

"Have you been here long, Countess?" he asked. "I'll come by to kiss your hand. I'm here on business and have brought my girls with me. They say Semenova acts marvelously. Count Pierre never used to forget us. Is he here?"
"Yes, he meant to come by," answered Helene, and glanced attentively at Natasha.
Count Rostov sat back down.
"Handsome, isn't she?" he whispered to Natasha.
"Wonderful!" answered Natasha. "She's a woman you could easily fall in love with."
Just then the last chords of the overture were heard and the conductor tapped his baton. Some latecomers took their seats in the stalls, and the curtain rose.

As soon as it rose, everyone in the boxes and stalls fell silent, and all the men, old and young, in uniform and evening dress, and all the women with jewels on their bare skin, turned their full attention with eager curiosity to the stage. Natasha too began to look at it.
